registers.role: sample frame and outcomes: deaths and exposures for the annual period life tables by sex and socio-economic group

registers.name_in_paper: individuals' income and wealth records used for the affluence measure of Cairns et al. (2019)
registers.years: 1984-2015 (lagged one year relative to the 1985-2016 life tables)
registers.role: treatment / stratifier: construction of the affluence index that assigns individuals to socio-economic quintiles
variables_mentioned: gross annual income, including wage income, unemployment benefits, social assistance and pension income
net wealth, defined as total assets minus total liabilities
assets: real property, bank deposits, stocks, bonds and cash holdings
liabilities: all types of debt to private companies and the government

linkages: Individuals are ranked by the affluence index A(j,x,y) = W(j,x-1,y-1) + K * I(j,x-1,y-1) with K = 15, so each person's register wealth and income of year y-1 at age x-1 are linked to their mortality exposure at age x in year y.
For married couples, wealth is assigned 50% to each spouse, which links spouses' wealth records.
Individuals may move between socio-economic groups before age 67 but are locked into the group they occupy at age 67, linking each later life-table observation to that group.

sample.universe: The Danish population observed in the population registers over 1985-2016, both sexes, at the ages relevant for retirement (from age 50 for the survival probabilities, from age 65 for the lifespan distributions, and from the retirement age for the life expectancy, entropy and annuity measures).
sample.unit_of_observation: Person-year, aggregated into annual sex-, age- and socio-economic-group-specific period life tables (one life table per sex, group and calendar year).
selection_rules: Use the newly developed affluence measure of Cairns et al. (2019), based on individuals' income and wealth, to divide the population into five socio-economic groups (quintiles) at each age and each point in time.
Rank individuals by affluence and split the total population into five equally sized quintiles G1 (low) to G5 (high).
Allow individuals to move between socio-economic groups but lock them into their assigned group at age 67, to avoid compositional effects between groups.
Compute annual period life tables for every single year from 1985 to 2016; the main figures pool the sexes for the total population (Fig. 1) and split by sex elsewhere.

construction_notes: Affluence index (Equation (1)): A(j,x,y) = W(j,x-1,y-1) + K * I(j,x-1,y-1), with K the capitalisation factor set to 15; Cairns et al. (2019) show the allocation is robust to K between 10 and 20.

Annual death rates are smoothed over the age axis by simulating 100,000 individual lifetimes from an exponential distribution with piece-wise constant rate (Willekens, 2009), repeated for every year 1985-2016; the authors state the result is equivalent to period life tables computed directly from observed death rates but yields continuous estimates of the force of mortality.
Current retirement age c: 67 during 1985-2004, 65 from 2004 onwards.
Target retirement age t: the age solving e(t) = 14.5, computed from the total population's life table with no distinction between the sexes; about 67 in 1985-1995 and 71.51 in 2016.
Remaining life expectancy e(x) by Equation (2); lifetable entropy H(x) = e-dagger(x)/e(x) by Equation (3).

Cost of a life annuity a-bar(x) by Equation (4): present value of payments of $1 made continuously per year from age x until death, no guarantee period, discounted at a constant force of interest delta; the baseline sets delta = 0 (so a-bar(x) = e(x)) and Fig. 8 uses 5%.
Entropy of the cost of a life annuity H-bar(x,delta) by Equation (5); at delta = 0 it equals H(x).
Relative differences to the total population by Equations (6) and (7).
Decomposition of the between-group difference in the relative change over time of H-bar(x,delta) into dispersion and translation components by Equation (12) of Appendix A.3.
Cohort robustness (Appendix A.4): period mortality rates by socio-economic group are forecast with the coherent Li and Lee (2005) method, reorganised by cohort, and dated by Year = Cohort + t_c.

claims.statement: Evaluating lifespan inequality at the target retirement age t, rather than at the current statutory age c, raises the lifetable entropy of the total Danish population: by the end of the study period H(t) had declined to 0.46 while H(c) had declined to 0.39.

treatment.label: Retirement age at which the measures are evaluated: the current statutory age c versus the target age t that is linked to life expectancy

definition.value: Two retirement-age rules applied to the same observed period life tables. c is the statutory old-age-pension age, 67 during 1985-2004 and 65 from 2004 onwards. t is the target retirement age of the 2007 Danish pension reform, defined as the age solving e(t) = 14.5, i.e. the age at which remaining life expectancy equals 14.5 years; t is about 67 in 1985-1995 and 71.51 in 2016.

timing.value: Each calendar year from 1985 to 2016; both ages are recomputed every year from that year's period life table of the total population.

outcome.label: Lifespan inequality after retirement: lifetable entropy H(x)

definition.value: Keyfitz lifetable entropy evaluated at the retirement age, H(x) = e-dagger(x) / e(x) (Equation (3)), where e-dagger(x) is the number of years of life lost due to death above age x. It is a relative measure of lifespan inequality bounded between 0 (everyone dies at the same age) and 1, and it does not depend on the level of mortality. It is evaluated at the retirement age itself: at x = c under the current pension scheme and at x = t under the target pension scheme.

timing.value: Computed from the period life table of each calendar year 1985-2016, at the retirement age of that year.

units.value: lifetable entropy (dimensionless index between 0 and 1)

magnitude.interpretation: "H (c ) is lower than H (t ), implying that lifespan inequality is lower after retirement age c than it is after age t" (p. 5); the authors read this as pensioners being more uncertain about the number of years they spend in retirement when they retire at age t.

A positive value means a higher annuity cost and hence higher expected pension benefits than the population average. At a zero force of interest a-bar(x) = e(x). Here computed from cohort rather than period data: period mortality rates by socio-economic group are forecast with the Li and Lee (2005) method and reorganised by cohort.

timing.value: Each calendar year 1985-2016, evaluated at the retirement age of that year; the caption of Fig. 5 does not state whether the current age c or the target age t is used, while Fig. 8 reports both.

units.value: percent difference in the annuity cost relative to the total population

magnitude.interpretation: With a higher interest rate the difference in survival matters less for the gap in the cost of the annuity (p. 9); at zero interest the annuity cost equals life expectancy.

estimand.target_population: Danish females and males by affluence quintile, compared with the total population, cohort basis.

population.description: The Danish population split by sex and into five affluence quintiles G1-G5, summarised by annual period life tables, 1985-2016.
population.ages: The retirement age at which the annuity starts; the caption of Fig. 5 does not state whether the current age c or the target age t is used (Fig. 8 reports both).
population.selection: The full register population of Denmark; individuals are ranked each year by the affluence index of Cairns et al. (2019) into five equally sized quintiles at each age and point in time, and are locked into the group they occupy at age 67.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. The force of interest entering the annuity calculation is set by the authors, to 0% in the baseline figure and to 5% in the appendix figure.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual period life tables (synthetic cohorts) describe the mortality regime faced at retirement; cohort mortality dynamics are not used in the main analysis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix A.4 repeats the analysis with cohort measures (Figs. 10 and 11) and reports that entropies and the socio-economic gap in life annuity factors are remarkably similar across the two perspectives (p. 8, p. 11).

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals may move between affluence quintiles before age 67 but are locked into the group they occupy at age 67, so the group-specific life tables condition on group membership fixed at that age.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors cite the sensitivity analysis of Kallestrup-Lamb et al. (2020): since 1985 only 6.1% of females moved up one group and 5.7% down one group each year, and moves of more than one group are negligible (less than 2%) (p. 3).

implies_edges.to: inclusion in a socio-economic group life table

key_assumptions.assumption: All individuals are assumed to have accumulated the same savings at retirement, to retire at the same retirement age (either c or t) and to face the same interest rate, so that differences between socio-economic groups in the cost of a life annuity and in its entropy arise solely through differences in the distribution of lifespans.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplification, with no supporting test (p. 4).

key_assumptions.assumption: The affluence index of Cairns et al. (2019), combining an individual's own lagged wealth and income with capitalisation factor K = 15, validly ranks individuals into five socio-economic groups that capture heterogeneity in longevity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors report that Cairns et al. (2019) show the allocation procedure is robust to choices of K in the interval from 10 to 20 and that K = 15 is a reasonable choice (p. 3).

key_assumptions.assumption: The pension is represented by a life annuity paying one monetary unit continuously per year from the retirement age until death, with no guarantee periods, discounted at a constant force of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the definition of the actuarial measures (p. 4); the baseline sets the force of interest to zero and Fig. 8 repeats the calculation at 5%.

key_assumptions.assumption: The cohort comparison requires period mortality rates by socio-economic group to be forecast with the Li-Lee (2005) method and then reorganised by cohort, so the cohort quantities depend on the validity of that projection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors concede that calculating cohort trends from forecasted data introduces uncertainty regarding the validity of the projection assumptions (p. 10).

threats_discussed: Period life tables are synthetic cohorts and may not describe the experience of any real cohort; the authors address this in Appendix A.4 with a cohort replication.
robustness_checks: A force of interest of 5% instead of 0% (Fig. 8 in Appendix A)
Cohort instead of period life tables, using Li and Lee (2005) mortality forecasts (Figs. 10 and 11 in Appendix A)
unresolved_confounders: The authors concede that calculating cohort trends from forecasted data introduces uncertainty regarding the validity of the assumptions used to project future demographic trends.

The outcome here is the magnitude of the socio-economic gap (the spread of the group series around the total-population line), which the authors say reduces and converges; the sign records that contraction, not a uniform downward shift of every group's relative difference.

evidence.annotation: Fig. 11. Relative differences in the financial cost of pensions by socio-economic group with respect to the total population. Calculations performed using a cohort trend. 1985-2016.

evidence.how: The paper reports no standard errors, confidence intervals or p-values anywhere: every reported quantity is a deterministic life-table or actuarial functional computed from register death counts, and all results are shown as figures without uncertainty bands.
The paper reports no sample size for any estimate: it uses the full Danish register population aggregated into annual period life tables and prints no count of individuals, deaths or person-years.
The force of interest is an assumption of the actuarial calculation, not a register variable.

The paper names no register or register variable; the annuity factors are computed from the paper's own life tables, which are built from register death counts described only as 'population registers' (abstract, p. 1).
The paper states this result in words only: no numerical value for it is printed in the text, in the figure annotation or in any table, and the figure carries no printed data labels.

The paper prints no reference or baseline level of this outcome for this claim: the figures show the group series against an unlabelled grey total-population line and no numerical value for it is given in the text, table note or figure annotation.
